shared_quiz_requirement_crosswalk.prompt: A patient with recurrent left leg pain nine months after L5/S1 microdiscectomy has soft tissue in the left anterior epidural space at the operated level. Explain how you would use contrast to decide whether this is fibrosis or recurrent disc material, and why the timing of the post-contrast images matters.
shared_quiz_requirement_crosswalk.authored_answer: Give gadolinium and image early, within roughly ten to fifteen minutes. Epidural fibrosis is vascularised granulation tissue: it enhances immediately, homogeneously and throughout its substance, and it tends to be retractile rather than mass-like, drawing the thecal sac and root towards it. Recurrent disc material is avascular and does not enhance itself; what enhances is the vascularised tissue around it, so on early images it shows a peripheral rim of enhancement with a non-enhancing centre, and it is polypoid, has mass effect, and is continuous with the disc space. The timing matters because contrast diffuses passively into disc material over time, so on images acquired thirty minutes or more after injection the recurrent disc fills in and becomes indistinguishable from scar, turning a reliable sign into a misleading one.

shared_quiz_requirement_crosswalk.prompt: Two patients each have a large central disc extrusion: one at T9/T10 and one at L4/L5. Explain what determines whether the picture is cord compression or cauda equina compression, what each looks like clinically, and how far the MRI must extend.
shared_quiz_requirement_crosswalk.authored_answer: The determinant is the level of the conus medullaris, which in adults ends at about T12 to L1, with the lower limit of normal around the L2/L3 disc; a compressive lesion above it presses on the cord, one below it presses on the cauda equina. The T9/T10 extrusion therefore causes cord compression, with upper motor neurone signs below the level: spasticity, brisk reflexes, extensor plantars, a sensory level, and T2 signal change within the cord if compression has been sustained. The L4/L5 extrusion compresses nerve roots and gives lower motor neurone signs: flaccid weakness, absent reflexes, bilateral radicular pain, saddle anaesthesia, and urinary retention with overflow incontinence. The MRI must cover the whole lumbosacral spine down to the sacrum, because a compressive lesion below the volume scanned is simply missed, and it must extend upwards whenever the signs are of cord rather than root disease, since the true upper level of the lesion may lie well above the symptomatic dermatome.

shared_quiz_requirement_crosswalk.prompt: A CT shows an L1 burst fracture in a neurologically intact patient, and the surgical team asks whether the posterior ligamentous complex is intact. State the sequence you would rely on, the findings that indicate disruption, and why the determination changes the plan.
shared_quiz_requirement_crosswalk.authored_answer: Sagittal STIR, or another fat-suppressed T2-weighted sequence; fat suppression is what makes ligamentous and interspinous oedema visible against fatty marrow and epidural fat. Disruption is indicated by high signal within or frank discontinuity of the supraspinous and interspinous ligaments and the ligamentum flavum, widening of the interspinous distance compared with the levels above and below, fluid or widening in the facet joints, a perched or dislocated facet, and avulsion at a ligamentous attachment. It changes the plan because the posterior ligamentous complex is the principal restraint against progressive kyphosis and translation: with it intact, a burst fracture in a neurologically intact patient is usually braced, and with it disrupted the same fracture scores into the operative range and is stabilised. CT can only infer the state of the ligaments from bony spacing, which is why MRI is added whenever the answer would change management.

MOGAD H-sign, infarct anterior horns and other gray-matter patterns overlap; require timing, actual paired DWI/ADC, antibodies and clinical data when relevant.

Shared Q3 precise early versus delayed contrast timings and management statements need current protocol/specialist validation; published myelopathy examples cannot certify postoperative lumbar scar/disc behavior.
Historical source glioblastoma terminology and imaging morphology do not establish a current integrated molecular tumour diagnosis or WHO grade.
